Three rulers can agree and still all be stretched. More readings help only when you know how the tools relate to what you are measuring.

Words used here
calibration
Checking how a measuring tool’s readings relate to a known reference.
Read the fuller explanation

The hidden-plane example does not say that any collection of extra channels will reveal the answer. The ports must reach the relevant subspace, and their relationship to the system must be calibrated. More readings are useful only if you know what they are readings of.

Imagine measuring a table with three rulers that all stretched in the same heat. Agreement would be reassuring. It would not supply the missing reference. This is an analogy for the question of access and calibration, not a further result of the finite model.

Before asking what the system did, ask what the apparatus could distinguish. Which states would still look identical through these ports? A blank region on that map is a reason to design another measurement.

Where this comes from: What a measuring tool can see

Finite model result

A result in a specified mathematical model

One reading can miss a changing part of the model. Several well-chosen, checked measurements can reveal it. This is not yet a physical measurement.

Read the full source note

Scalar impedance and dark holonomy

In the finite witness, the scalar port e₄ is orthogonal to the moving dark plane. Its response is independent of the loop parameter. Full matrix residues recover the projector; a calibrated sufficiently ranked port set is needed experimentally.
